title: Montana’s plan to become an experimental medical hub just pushed forward
gist: Montana's newly finalized rules let any biotech whose drug cleared preliminary testing pay $12,500 to a privately run review board, then sell the unapproved drug at any price it chooses through in-state clinics — with the first clinic due around year-end. The law was drafted by longevity investors, the review board is funded by applicant fees and staffed from their own network, and early demand is coming from oncology and neurodegenerative disease rather than anti-aging.

themes.theme: A commercial pathway around the FDA

insights.claim: As of this week in Montana, any biotech company holding an experimental drug has a clear path to selling it directly to consumers without FDA approval.
insights.so_what: A US state has created a legal retail channel for pre-approval drugs — a genuinely new revenue line for cash-starved clinical-stage biotechs.
insights.quote: any biotech company with an experimental drug has a clear path to selling it to consumers
insights.locator: As of this week in Montana
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The mechanics are specific: drugs that have been through preliminary testing, sometimes in as few as 10 healthy people, qualify; the company pays $12,500 to apply to a review board; and once approved it sets its own price and sells through experimental treatment clinics.
insights.so_what: A $12,500 gate versus hundreds of millions for a full approval path is the arbitrage that will attract applicants.
insights.quote: Companies whose drugs have been through preliminary testing—sometimes in as few as 10 healthy people—can pay $12,500 to apply to a newly established review board for approval.
insights.locator: Companies whose drugs have been through
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Montana's law is unique because other jurisdictions with right-to-try statutes restrict access to the terminally ill, whereas Montana theoretically opens access to anyone who gives informed consent and can pay.
insights.so_what: Removing the terminal-illness gate converts a compassionate-use carve-out into an addressable consumer market including the worried well and longevity buyers.
insights.quote: in Montana access is theoretically available to anyone who gives informed consent and can pay
insights.locator: Montana’s latest right-to-try legislation is unique
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The state's Department of Health and Human Services finalized implementing rules that took effect from Saturday, July 25, after a long delay that had stalled the whole program.
entities: Department of Health and Human Services
insights.so_what: The regulatory starting gun has fired — the operational timeline from here is measured in months, not years.
insights.quote: Then on Friday, we heard they were effective … from Saturday [July 25]
insights.locator: The rules have been taking a very long time
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The first experimental treatment clinic is likely to be operating around the end of this year, with treatment rooms being outfitted and medical directors being hired now.
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term catalyst date for anyone tracking the first commercial sale of an unapproved drug in the US.
insights.quote: Treatment rooms are being outfitted. Medical directors are being hired.
insights.locator: While Montana’s first ETRB prepares
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: Longevity capital as the political author of the law

insights.claim: Unlike the broader US movement to widen access to unapproved drugs, Montana's law was driven and drafted by longevity enthusiasts rather than the usual libertarian and patient advocacy groups.
insights.so_what: Longevity money has become a legislative actor, not just a research funder — expect the same playbook attempted in other states.
insights.quote: It’s been driven and drafted by longevity enthusiasts instead of the usual libertarian and patient groups.
insights.locator: There has been a growing movement
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The sequence was incremental: Montana passed a right-to-try law in 2015, expanded it in 2023 beyond terminal patients with state senator Ken Bogner's support, then passed a second bill in April 2025 specifying how clinics can sell unapproved drugs.
insights.so_what: A three-step legislative ratchet is the template competitors and opponents will study; each step alone looked minor.
insights.locator: An unusual origin story
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The Alliance for Longevity Initiatives approached the state senator after he had already started drafting, then connected him with people who helped write the bill and testified for it.
insights.so_what: Shows the lobbying mechanism: a small nonprofit converting a sympathetic legislator into a national regulatory precedent.
insights.locator: Bogner says he had “started working on a bill”
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The legislative intent was explicitly preventive rather than therapeutic, focusing on preventative medicine rather than just treating diseases once they show up.
insights.so_what: Preventive framing is what makes healthy-consumer sales legally coherent — and is where the largest potential market sits.
insights.quote: more on preventative medicine
insights.locator: Last year, Bogner told MIT Technology Review
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Tech entrepreneur Niklas Anzinger shifted his regulatory-arbitrage project from the private Honduran charter city of Próspera to Montana on the reasoning that Montana builds on existing regulatory precedents.
insights.so_what: The charter-city medical-tourism model is migrating onshore into US states, where credibility and payment rails are far stronger.
insights.quote: Now we think that Montana is a better model, because it’s building on … existing regulatory precedents
insights.locator: Over the last couple of years
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Anzinger says he worked with a handful of unnamed biotech companies to draft the second bill that set the terms under which clinics can offer unapproved drugs.
insights.so_what: The commercial rules were written by prospective participants, which predicts a permissive interpretation in practice.
insights.locator: Once Montana’s 2023 law was passed
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: Who actually holds the gatekeeping power

insights.claim: The state's first and currently only review board, the Montana ETRB, was established and announced by Infinita rather than by the state, and other groups remain free to set up competing boards.
insights.so_what: Approval authority is privatized and contestable — a race between rival boards could compete standards downward.
insights.locator: The first step was to establish
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Infinita pays board members a flat fee funded by the same $12,500 application fees the companies pay, while asserting that board members and their decisions are independent of Infinita.
insights.so_what: The reviewer is paid by applicant volume — the classic incentive structure behind rating-agency style approval inflation.
insights.quote: Infinita will pay board members a flat fee, funded by the $12,500 companies will have to pay to have their applications reviewed.
insights.locator: Infinita will pay board members
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: After the bill's own sponsoring senator objected that the board's website wrongly implied it was an official state body, the site was amended to disclose that it is a private service run by Montana Governance Services Inc., an entity under the Infinita umbrella.
insights.so_what: Early positioning already blurred public and private authority — a reputational and legal risk that could invite state intervention.
insights.quote: It is a private service run by Montana Governance Services Inc.
insights.locator: After Bogner raised concerns
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The board's composition satisfies the rules on paper — a Montana-licensed oncologist and a bioethicist — but the bioethicist is a libertarian known for strong pro-self-medication views and the author of Pharmaceutical Freedom.
insights.so_what: Formal compliance with an ethics requirement does not imply an adversarial check; expect high approval rates.
insights.locator: In accordance with the rules
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Three of the five board seats went to figures recruited from Infinita's own longevity network, including a former senior NIH aging official who was chief scientific officer at the Saudi-backed Hevolution Foundation, the former head of the Dog Aging Project, and the executive director of the $101 million X Prize Healthspan competition.
insights.so_what: Maps the concentrated network that now controls a de facto drug-approval channel, and shows Gulf-linked longevity money adjacent to it.
insights.quote: When we looked at our own network, these were some of the best guys
insights.locator: The other three members are familiar faces
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: A board member who has publicly criticized unproven peptide and stem-cell sales frames Montana as a more regulated environment offering scientific oversight, informed consent, and data collection.
insights.so_what: The legitimacy pitch is harm reduction versus the existing grey market, not versus the FDA — a framing worth testing against outcomes.
insights.quote: It will be done in a very rigorous way, with qualified medical professionals and appropriate oversight
insights.locator: Supporters of the law stress
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: Early demand: oncology and neuro, not longevity

insights.claim: Despite the law's longevity origins, initial interest is coming disproportionately from oncology and neurodegenerative disease, which surprised the organizers themselves.
insights.so_what: The realized market is severe-disease desperation, not anti-aging consumers — repointing where the first revenue and first controversies will land.
insights.quote: We were actually surprised that much of the interest … is actually more from oncology [and] neurodegenerative disease
insights.locator: Applications incoming
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Two applications have already been submitted to the newly formed board, from biotech companies developing drugs for neuropathy and for hearing loss.
insights.so_what: Concrete deal flow within days of the rules taking effect signals pent-up supply, not a hypothetical market.
insights.locator: Martin says that two applications
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: One applicant, WinSanTor, has a phase II peripheral neuropathy drug, a newsletter reaching around 15,000 patients, and a CEO who says he regularly receives messages from people desperate enough to be suicidal.
insights.so_what: An existing patient mailing list is the distribution asset that makes this channel commercially viable overnight.
insights.quote: We have a newsletter [that is sent to] around 15,000 patients
insights.locator: One of the applications was submitted
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The applicant intends to collect data from Montana patients that might help accelerate the drug's formal approval, while still continuing conventional clinical trials.
insights.so_what: If real-world Montana data ever counts toward approval, the pathway becomes a trial-acceleration tool rather than just a revenue channel — a much bigger structural change.
insights.locator: He hopes that not only will he be able
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: FDA risk versus the expanded-access alternative

insights.claim: A French biotech CEO calls Montana's system very interesting, very pragmatic, and suitable for his drug, yet will not apply because a bad outcome in Montana could jeopardize his standing with the FDA.
insights.so_what: FDA relationship risk, not law or demand, is the binding constraint on participation — the key variable determining whether this scales.
insights.quote: very interesting and very pragmatic
insights.locator: But not all biotech companies
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Organizers asked the FDA for assurance that participating companies would not be penalized later and received nothing beyond a restatement of the federal Right to Try Act, with the agency saying it does not comment on state legislation as a matter of policy.
insights.so_what: Regulatory silence is the overhang; an explicit FDA statement either way would be the single biggest catalyst for or against this market.
insights.quote: As a matter of policy, the FDA does not comment on state legislation
insights.locator: Martin and others have asked the FDA
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Even an FDA assurance would offer weak long-term protection because the agency's position can shift with a new presidential administration.
insights.so_what: Political duration risk means any company underwriting a Montana strategy is taking an unhedgeable multi-year regulatory bet.
insights.quote: I wouldn’t bet on anything that the FDA is saying today being applicable when the rubber hits the road later
insights.locator: Even if the FDA were to provide
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: The premise that the FDA blocks access is contested by data: the agency approves over 99% of expanded-access applications and says the form takes less than 45 minutes to complete.
insights.so_what: If the bottleneck story is false, the real product Montana sells is pricing freedom rather than access — which reframes the whole business case.
insights.quote: The FDA isn’t a bottleneck but in fact exists to help ensure that expanded-access programs are aboveboard
insights.locator: The FDA approves over 99%
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: Pricing power is the actual innovation

insights.claim: Under federal expanded access companies may charge only the costs of making, transporting, and monitoring a drug and must justify the price to the FDA, whereas in Montana they can charge whatever they want.
insights.so_what: Unconstrained pricing on unapproved assets is the economic core of the law; it converts compassionate use into a P&L line.
insights.quote: In Montana, they can charge whatever price they want.
insights.locator: Kaeberlein also highlights another key difference
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Montana's design deliberately creates not just a legal pathway for patients but a business model that companies may actually be willing to use.
insights.so_what: The stated goal is commercial adoption, which is the metric to track — application counts, not patient counts.
insights.quote: Instead of simply creating a legal pathway for patients, it also creates a business model that companies may actually be willing to use
insights.locator: Instead of simply creating a legal pathway
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Intentions on price already diverge sharply: one applicant plans to sell at cost while the reluctant French CEO says he would prefer market pricing, hinting at rare-disease drug levels where the recent median price was $218,872.
insights.so_what: A ~$219k anchor on pre-approval drugs sets the revenue upside that will draw in less scrupulous entrants.
insights.quote: In recent years, the median price of such drugs was $218,872.
insights.locator: When asked what that might be
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

themes.theme: Safety base rates and the harm case

insights.claim: Phase I trials do not conclusively establish safety, and around 17% of drugs are found to be inadequately safe during phase III trials — after the stage Montana treats as sufficient.
insights.so_what: A roughly one-in-six late-stage safety failure rate quantifies the harm exposure and the litigation tail sitting under this market.
insights.quote: Around 17% of drugs are found to be inadequately safe during phase III trials.
insights.locator: Phase I trials don’t conclusively reveal
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: A Harvard drug-regulation expert says the belief that a drug is proven safe because it passed a phase I study is very, very wrong, and voices concern about selling unproven treatments without FDA oversight.
insights.so_what: The expert consensus against the model is the source of future headline risk that could trigger state-level rollback.
insights.quote: The idea that a drug has been proven safe because it’s been subject to a phase I study is very, very wrong
insights.locator: The idea that a drug has been proven safe
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou

insights.claim: Companies that want to stay on good terms with the FDA would be safest taking the expanded-access route rather than Montana's, according to a health law specialist.
insights.so_what: Predicts adverse selection: the firms most likely to use Montana are those with the least to lose with the FDA.
insights.locator: Companies that want to stay on good terms
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
